The new musical by Michael R. Jackson performs a phenomenal feat — it is both a raw and unflinching interrogation of identity and the most furiously entertaining show on Broadway.

And yet, it seems as if there is no measure of praise that could be too much; after all, this is a show that allows a Black gay man to be vulnerable onstage without dismissing or fetishizing his trauma, desires and creative ambitions.
An intimate and personal exploration of the tangled interior life of a black gay man, it represents theater at its most daring and unexpected.

That is Jackson’s most awe-inspiring accomplishment with A Strange Loop, which is certainly the best new musical on Broadway this season: he has created a finely honed piece of theater while always remaining true to his own distinct voice.
What Jackson has created with A Strange Loop is nothing short of astounding.
In being crafted so individually, Usher emerges as the most bruised and honest Broadway hero on stage right now, taking a Broadway audience on an equally honest and bruising journey.
Michael R. Jackson's musical is a bold, brilliant and deeply personal work
But sadly, those who favor form over substance will miss out on the singular brilliance of this unusual piece.
At the Lyceum, it feels like a seismic event. When was the last time Broadway saw a musical as brazenly original and brutally candid as this?

In proving that they do, and in bringing Usher’s vivid and complex inner life all the way to Broadway with such gripping vibrancy, Jackson nudges the musical theater form in a startling, new direction.
The changes since Off-Broadway have resulted in a crisper production with a more elaborate design on an obviously bigger budget.
It is a humdinger of a show that takes place at a funeral service for a cousin who has died of AIDS.
This black gay man wandering around New York wondering why life is so terrible – that man himself is a voice in all our heads.
Michael R. Jackson's Pulitzer Prize-winning musical is a raw, uncompromising work of art that challenges audiences while delivering moments of profound beauty and devastating honesty.
A Strange Loop is a fascinatingly original addition to the Broadway season.

"The standard advice for aspiring authors is 'Write about what you know.' In the case of 'A Strange Loop,' both librettist-composer-lyricist Michael R. Jackson, and his motley but magical protagonist Usher, have chosen to write about what they want to know: namely, the key to identity; the answer to the age-old riddle of human consciousness.

“A Strange Loop” ultimately falls victim to the perils of its own design, becoming so messy, whiny, confrontational, sexually explicit, and theoretical that it will probably turn off many theatergoers while invigorating and thrilling plenty of others.
A Strange Loop is highly polished, and Jaquel Spivey, taking on the role created by Larry Owens, defines the term tour-de-force by his exceptional acting and singing.
A Strange Loop also has graphic depictions of sex, some blasphemous representations of religion and lots of profanity, including the n-word.

cn.t: Michael R. Jackson's Pulitzer-winning musical earns overwhelming praise as a brazenly original, brutally honest exploration of Black queer identity that feels revolutionary for Broadway, though its raw explicitness and self-referential structure occasionally test some critics.

vs.sum: The Lyceum Theatre offers good sightlines and a charming Beaux Arts ambiance, but suffers from cramped seating and small restrooms. Ideal for intimate dramas, but patrons should be prepared for less comfort during their visit.

acc.note: 4 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No elevator. Infrared devices available.
